title: Packages, modules and the toolchain
summary: How code is organized, how versions are chosen, and the commands worth knowing.

concepts.title: Packages and imports
concepts.brief:
A package is a **directory**. Every file in it declares the same `package` name, and they share one namespace — no imports between files of the same package, and an unexported identifier is visible across all of them.

**Import cycles are a hard compile error.** Two packages cannot import each other, even indirectly. That forces a layered design and is one of the stronger opinions in the language.

A directory named **`internal`** is special: only code rooted at its parent can import it. It is the one real access control Go has above the exported/unexported line, and it is enforced by the compiler.

examples.label: internal is enforced, not a convention
examples.code:
github.com/you/app/
  main.go                  -> can import internal/db
  internal/
    db/db.go               -> importable only within github.com/you/app/...
  pkg/
    client/client.go       -> importable by anyone
examples.note: Someone else importing `github.com/you/app/internal/db` gets a compile error. It is how you publish a module without freezing its guts as public API.

examples.label: init(), and when it runs
examples.note: Dependencies initialize first, depth-first. `import _ "net/http/pprof"` imports a package purely so its `init()` registers HTTP handlers.

items.prompt: Package `a` imports `b`, and you add an import of `a` to `b`.
choices: A compile error — cycles are forbidden, however indirect
It compiles; the linker resolves the cycle
It compiles with a vet warning
It compiles only if one of them uses an interface
items.explain: Hard error, and it is the constraint that shapes Go project layout most. The usual resolutions: move the shared type into a third package that both import, or define an interface in the consumer so the dependency only points one way. Reaching for the second one is how most Go code ends up testable.

choices: Only code under github.com/you/app/
Anyone — internal is a naming convention only
Only files in the same directory
Only the main package of that module
items.explain: Anything rooted at `internal`'s parent, enforced by the compiler. This is how you publish a library without every helper becoming public API you can never change. If you are unsure whether to export something, putting it in `internal` keeps the option open.

items.prompt: Two files in the same directory, same `package store`. Does `a.go` need to import `b.go` to call its unexported function?
choices: No — files in one package share a namespace; imports are per-package
Yes, with a relative import
Yes, and the function must be exported
Only if they are compiled separately
items.explain: The package is the unit, not the file. Splitting a package across files is purely organizational, and unexported identifiers are visible to all of them. There are no relative imports in Go, and no way to import one file from another.

choices: It runs that package's init(), which registers the debug HTTP handlers
It imports it lazily, only if something references it
It suppresses the unused-import error for a package you plan to use
It imports only the package's types, not its functions
items.explain: A blank import is for side effects: you want the `init()` to run and have no need to name anything. Database drivers work the same way — `import _ "github.com/lib/pq"` registers "postgres" with `database/sql`. It is also why deleting an import that "isn't used" can break a program at runtime.

concepts.title: Modules and versions
concepts.brief:
A module is a tree of packages with a `go.mod` at its root declaring the module path, the language version, and its requirements.

Go picks versions by **Minimal Version Selection**: for each dependency it takes the **highest version anyone explicitly asked for**, and nothing newer. There is no solver and no floating range, so a build is reproducible without a lockfile — `go.sum` holds checksums for verification, not version choices.

**Major versions are part of the import path.** v2 and above append `/v2`, so `example.com/lib` and `example.com/lib/v2` are different packages that can coexist in one build.

examples.label: go.mod
examples.code:
module github.com/you/app

go 1.22

require (
	github.com/go-chi/chi/v5 v5.0.12
	golang.org/x/sync v0.7.0
)
examples.note: The `go` directive is not just metadata: it selects language semantics, which is how the Go 1.22 loop-variable change could ship without breaking old modules.

examples.label: The commands that edit it
examples.code:
$ go mod init github.com/you/app   # create it
$ go get example.com/lib@v1.4.0    # add or change a requirement
$ go mod tidy                      # add what is used, drop what is not
$ go mod why example.com/lib       # why is this here at all
examples.note: `go mod tidy` is the one to run before committing: it reconciles go.mod and go.sum with what the code actually imports.

items.prompt: Your module needs lib v1.2.0. A dependency needs lib v1.4.0. v1.9.0 exists. Which is built?
choices: v1.4.0 — the highest version explicitly required by anyone
v1.9.0 — the latest compatible release
v1.2.0 — your own requirement wins
The build fails with a version conflict
items.explain: Minimal Version Selection takes the maximum of the *requested* versions and never upgrades on its own. So adding a dependency cannot silently move your other dependencies forward, and a build today produces the same binary as a build last year. Upgrades only happen when you run `go get`.

items.prompt: A library releases v2.0.0. What changes for you?
choices: The import path gains a /v2 suffix — it is effectively a different package
Nothing; go.mod records the major version
You must delete go.sum and re-resolve
Go refuses v2+ unless you opt in with GOFLAGS
items.explain: Semantic import versioning: the major version lives in the path. The upside is that two incompatible majors can coexist in one build, so a dependency upgrading to v2 does not force you to. The cost is that upgrading means editing every import line — which `go mod tidy` will not do for you.

choices: Checksums that verify downloaded modules are unchanged — not version selection
A lockfile pinning the resolved version of every dependency
A cache of downloaded module archives
A list of modules permitted by your organization
items.explain: Integrity, not resolution. `go.mod` plus MVS already makes the build reproducible, so `go.sum` exists to detect a module whose contents changed under a tag you already use. Commit it — a mismatch is a supply-chain signal, and a missing entry fails the build.

items.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
pairs: Create go.mod for a new module
Sync requirements with what the code imports
Explain which import pulls it in
items.explain: `go mod why` is the one people forget, and it is what you want when `go.mod` has grown something nobody recognizes — it prints the import chain from your code to that module.

concepts.title: The toolchain and the binary
concepts.brief:
`go build` produces a **single self-contained binary** with the runtime linked in. No interpreter, no shared libraries to match, no base image beyond what your own code needs. That property is why so much infrastructure software is written in Go.

The caveat is **cgo**. Some standard packages — notably `net` and `os/user` — have C-backed implementations that get used by default on some systems, which links against libc and breaks `FROM scratch`. `CGO_ENABLED=0` forces the pure Go versions.

Cross-compiling needs no toolchain install: set `GOOS` and `GOARCH`.

examples.label: A binary that runs on an empty image
examples.code:
$ CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -o app .

$ cat Dockerfile
FROM scratch
COPY app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
examples.note: Without CGO_ENABLED=0 this can fail at runtime with 'no such file or directory' — which is the dynamic loader missing, not your binary.

examples.label: The commands worth muscle memory
examples.code:
$ go test ./...            # every package
$ go test -race ./...      # with the race detector
$ go test -run TestFoo     # one test by regex
$ go vet ./...             # the checks the compiler does not do
$ gofmt -l .               # list files that are not formatted
examples.note: `go test` runs a reduced set of vet checks first, so `go vet ./...` separately in CI is still worth it.

items.prompt: Your Go binary works locally, and in a `FROM scratch` image it exits with 'no such file or directory' — though the binary is clearly there.
choices: It was built with cgo, so it needs a dynamic loader the image does not have
The binary was built for the wrong GOARCH
scratch images cannot run ENTRYPOINT without a shell
The binary needs the execute bit set
items.explain: That message is the kernel failing to find the *interpreter* named in the ELF header, not the binary. A cgo build links dynamically against libc, which `scratch` does not have. Build with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, or use a base image with libc. `file app` or `ldd app` tells you which kind you have.

items.prompt: Which two environment variables select the target platform for `go build`?
items.explain: `GOOS` and `GOARCH`. Cross-compiling needs nothing installed — `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build` works from a Mac with no container. That falls apart the moment cgo is involved, which is another reason `CGO_ENABLED=0` is the common default in CI.

items.prompt: Match each go test flag to what it does.
pairs: Instruments memory access to find data races
Runs only tests matching a regex
Runs benchmarks as well as tests
items.explain: `-count=1` is the idiomatic way to force a re-run, because Go caches successful test results and a cached pass looks identical to a real one. `-race` roughly halves speed and raises memory, so it usually runs on CI rather than on every local save.

items.prompt: Why does Go have no formatting style debate?
choices: gofmt defines one canonical format, with essentially no options
The compiler rejects code that is not formatted
Each module sets its own style in go.mod
The language grammar makes only one layout valid
items.explain: `gofmt` has no style knobs, so there is nothing to argue about and every Go codebase looks the same. It compiles fine unformatted — the enforcement is cultural plus CI. `gofmt -l .` listing any file is the usual gate, and `goimports` does the same thing while fixing the import block.
